chunks: What a debugger is. The question: What is a debugger?
A debugger lets you control and watch a program while it runs on the real chip.
You can pause the processor, step through the code one line at a time, and look at variables, registers and memory.
It is a chain of three parts: debugger software on your PC, a small probe that plugs in over USB, and debug hardware built into the chip.
Imagine a film with a pause button and a magnifying glass. You can freeze the picture, advance one frame at a time, and inspect every prop on the set.
A debugger does this for a running program.
The picture breaks down in one place: pausing a real machine, such as a motor driver, can leave its outputs stuck in whatever state they were in.
The probe talks to the on-chip debug access port, which can reach the core's debug registers and, through the bus, any memory or peripheral register.
The comparators in the FPB and DWT blocks are what cause the core to halt.
Breakpoint: a marker that stops the program when it reaches a chosen line. Debug probe: the small hardware box that connects your PC to the chip's debug pins.
SWD / JTAG: two kinds of debug connection. SWD uses two signal wires and JTAG uses four or five.
Register: ("What registers are"): a small storage spot in the CPU or in a peripheral, which you can inspect while stopped.
Single-step: running just one line or instruction and stopping again.
You set a breakpoint on the line that updates a variable called count . You press run. The program runs at full speed until it reaches that line, and then the chip halts.
Your PC shows count = 7 . You single-step one line, and it now shows count = 8 . Inside the chip, a hardware comparator watches the addresses of instructions being fetched.
When one matches, it halts the processor. Chips have only about four to eight of these comparators. That is the whole idea.
"A debugger lets me control and inspect a program running on the microcontroller: halt it, step through code, set breakpoints, and read or modify variables, registers and memory.
It's a chain of host software, a USB debug probe, a two-wire SWD or four-wire JTAG link, and dedicated debug hardware inside the chip with a few breakpoint comparators.
The same link programs flash. Its limit is that halting is intrusive for real-time systems."
